\chapter{The One It Is Done To}
\label{ch:ta-ai}
\hlchaptermodality{86}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can mark the object of a verb with -ai, say me and you as objects, and tell when the ending is compulsory and when it is a choice that means 'the'.}

From cold: the accusative ending and which end of the word it sits on, the two pronoun objects and the changed bodies they stand on, and the one question — is the object a person — that decides whether the ending may be left off.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[-ai]{-\ta{ஐ} — your second case ending}

\label{lesson:TA-C86-ai}



\begin{quote}
Your first case ending was \textbf{-\ta{உக்கு}}, and what it taught was bigger than its meaning: English puts a word in front, Tamil sticks a piece on the back.

Here is the second piece, and it goes on the same end.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: -\ta{ஐ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{-\ta{ஐ}} — \emph{-ai} — \textbf{marks the one the verb is done to}
\end{quote}

A sentence can have two people in it, and something has to say which of them is doing and which is being done to. \textbf{English uses position}: \emph{the teacher saw the child} and \emph{the child saw the teacher} are built from the same three words and mean opposite things, and the only signal is the order.

\textbf{Tamil marks the one being done to}, and then the order stops carrying the weight:

\begin{quote}
\ta{நான்} \textbf{\ta{அவரை}} \ta{நினைக்கிறேன்}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{nāṉ \textbf{avarai} ninaikkiṟēṉ} — \textquotedblleft{}I think of them\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ta{அவர்}} became \textbf{\ta{அவரை}}. Nothing else moved. The verb you already know from the thinking chapter did not change, and \emph{nāṉ} is still optional because the \emph{-ēṉ} on the end is already saying \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: where the two endings sit}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the word} & \textbf{+ ending} & \textbf{what it says} \\
\midrule
\ta{அவர்} & \ta{அவர்}\textbf{\ta{உக்கு}} $\to$ \textbf{\ta{அவருக்கு}} & to them, for them \\
\ta{அவர்} & \ta{அவர்}\textbf{\ta{ஐ}} $\to$ \textbf{\ta{அவரை}} & them, as the one it is done to \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two endings, one place to put them, and the noun underneath is the same word both times. \textbf{A case ending in Tamil is a seam you can see}, which is the thing the dative chapter said was the biggest structural fact about the language — and this is the second piece of evidence for it rather than a new idea.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}avar … avarai\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nāṉ avarai ninaikkiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{}
  \item which word in that sentence is the one being thought of, and how you can tell
  \item \textquotedblleft{}avarukku\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}avarai\textquotedblright{} one after the other, and what each of them does
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{-\ta{ஐ}} mark? (\textbf{The one the verb is done to}.) Where does it go? (\textbf{On the end of the word}, like every Tamil case ending.) What is \emph{avar} as the one it is done to? (\emph{\textbf{Avarai}}.) And what does English use instead of an ending here? (\textbf{Position} — which word comes first.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[eṉṉai / uṉṉai]{\ta{என்னை} / \ta{உன்னை} — the body you already changed once}

\label{lesson:TA-C86-ennai-unnai}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}to me\textquotedblright{}. Then say the word for \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} on its own.

They do not look like each other, and the dative chapter told you why: the pronoun changes its body before an ending lands on it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{என்னை} and \ta{உன்னை}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{என்னை}} — \emph{eṉṉai} — \textbf{me}, as the one it is done to \textbf{\ta{உன்னை}} — \emph{uṉṉai} — \textbf{you}, as the one it is done to
\end{quote}

\textbf{These cost you nothing new.} You changed \emph{nāṉ} into \emph{eṉ-} to build \emph{enakku} chapters ago. That changed body is the same one \textbf{-\ta{ஐ}} lands on:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the word} & \textbf{to / for} & \textbf{the one it is done to} \\
\midrule
\ta{நான்} \emph{nāṉ} — I & \ta{எனக்கு} \emph{enakku} & \ta{என்னை} \emph{eṉṉai} \\
\ta{நீ} \emph{nī} — you & \ta{உனக்கு} \emph{unakku} & \ta{உன்னை} \emph{uṉṉai} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read down the middle column and then down the right one. \textbf{The left part of each word never changes once you have it.} Learning the body is the work; the endings are the cheap part, and there are only so many of them.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{என்னை} \ta{நினை}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{eṉṉai ninai} — \textquotedblleft{}think of me\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

A bare verb stem is already a command — you met that with \emph{pō!} in the farewell chapter — so this is a whole sentence with no machinery you have not used.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}enakku … eṉṉai\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}unakku … uṉṉai\textquotedblright{}
  \item the part of those four words that never changes
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eṉṉai ninai\textquotedblright{} — think of me
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{me}, as the one it is done to? (\emph{\textbf{Eṉṉai}}.) And \emph{to me}? (\emph{\textbf{Enakku}}.) What do those two have in common? (\textbf{The changed body \emph{eṉ-}}.) Which of the two endings would you put on it to say \textquotedblleft{}for you\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{-\ta{உக்கு}}, on \emph{uṉ-}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tēnīr / tēnīrai]{\ta{தேநீர்} / \ta{தேநீரை} — when the ending is a choice}

\label{lesson:TA-C86-rational}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}I think of them\textquotedblright{}. Say which piece of that sentence marks the one being thought of.

Now the part nobody tells you: that piece is not always required.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a person must have it, a thing need not}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{அவரை}} \ta{நினைக்கிறேன்} — I think of \textbf{them}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{தேநீர்}} \ta{வாங்குகிறேன்} — I buy tea
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{தேநீரை}} \ta{வாங்குகிறேன்} — I buy \textbf{the} tea
\end{quote}

\textbf{On a person the ending is obligatory.} Leaving it off does not make a casual sentence; it makes a broken one.

\textbf{On a thing it is a choice}, and the choice carries meaning. Bare \textbf{\ta{தேநீர்}} is tea in general, the kind of thing you buy. \textbf{\ta{தேநீரை}} is \emph{that} tea, a particular one already in view. Tamil has no word for \emph{the}, and this is one of the places the job gets done instead.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the object is} & \textbf{the ending} \\
\midrule
a person & required \\
a thing, in general & usually left off \\
a thing, a particular one & put on \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=violet!6,colframe=violet!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Across the family: the same line, drawn at the other end}]
Spanish draws this line too, and a Spanish learner has met it: \emph{veo la casa} (\textquotedblleft{}I see the house\textquotedblright{}) against \emph{veo \textbf{a} María} (\textquotedblleft{}I see María\textquotedblright{}). A human object gets a marker; a thing does not.

\textbf{Spanish puts that marker in front of the word as a separate piece. Tamil sticks it on the back.} Same distinction between a person and a thing, opposite end of the word — which is the difference the dative chapter opened with, now showing up in a second place.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}avarai ninaikkiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tēnīr vāṅgugiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{} and then \textquotedblleft{}tēnīrai vāṅgugiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{}
  \item which of those two is about a particular tea
  \item which of the three objects could not drop the ending, and why
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
When is \textbf{-\ta{ஐ}} obligatory? (\textbf{When the object is a person}.) What does putting it on a thing add? (\textbf{That it is a particular one} — Tamil has no word for \emph{the}.) And where does Spanish put its marker for a human object? (\textbf{In front}, as a separate word, where Tamil puts it on the back.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ai ninaivu]{(the one it is done to) — from cold}

\label{lesson:TA-R86-ai-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say the ending that marks the one a verb is done to, and say which end of the word it goes on.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one ending, one question}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the object} & \textbf{with the ending} & \textbf{required?} \\
\midrule
\ta{அவர்} — that person & \ta{அவரை} & yes \\
\ta{நான்} — I & \ta{என்னை} & yes \\
\ta{நீ} — you & \ta{உன்னை} & yes \\
\ta{தேநீர்} — tea & \ta{தேநீரை} & only for a particular one \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Three of the four rows are people, and people have no choice.} The question to ask of an object is not \emph{is this the subject or the object} — the ending answers that — but \textbf{is this a person}.

Two things carry over from earlier chapters rather than being new here. The pronouns stand on the changed bodies \textbf{eṉ-} and \textbf{uṉ-} that the dative built. And the ending sits on the back of the word, which is what your first case ending taught and what separates this language from the one that would put a word in front.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four objects in the table, each with its ending
  \item \textquotedblleft{}avarai ninaikkiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}eṉṉai ninai\textquotedblright{}
  \item which row of the table lets you choose, and what choosing adds
  \item the two words that share the body eṉ-
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{them}, as the one it is done to? (\emph{\textbf{Avarai}}.) What is \emph{me}? (\emph{\textbf{Eṉṉai}}.) When may the ending be left off? (\textbf{On a thing, when it is not a particular one}.) And what has to be true before it is compulsory? (\textbf{The object is a person}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yār uḷḷē, yār veḷiyē]{(\ta{இவர்}, \ta{விடை}, and the two we-words) — one idea in four places}

\label{lesson:TA-R86-who-is-in-the-room}



\begin{quote}
Introduce the person standing beside you as your friend.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the two words for we}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{who it covers} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{நாம்}} & me, and \textbf{you too} \\
\textbf{\ta{நாங்கள்}} & me and my people, \textbf{but not you} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English has one \emph{we} and leaves the listener guessing. Tamil makes you choose before you open your mouth, and the choice is audible to everyone in the room.

Getting it wrong is not a grammar slip — it either includes somebody you meant to exclude or shuts out somebody standing right there.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{இவர்}, and the ending that judges}
\textbf{\ta{இவர்} \ta{என்} \ta{நண்பர்}} — \emph{this is my friend} — is three words with no verb in the middle, the same silence the name sentence had.

What it adds is a \textbf{choice of ending}. \textbf{\ta{நண்பர்}} carries respect; a plainer ending would not. Introducing someone in Tamil therefore states your regard for them out loud, in front of them, whether or not you meant to say anything about it.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{விடை}}
\textbf{\ta{விடை}} is \emph{leave to depart} — a noun for the act of taking your leave, sharing a root with \textbf{\ta{வீடு}}, the house.

Set it beside the farewells: the everyday one promises a return, and this word names the departure itself. Tamil has both, and it reserves the naming one for the heavier moment.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Page covered.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item which we-word takes the listener in
  \item which one shuts them out
  \item \emph{this is my friend}, respectfully
  \item what the ending on that last word tells the listener
  \item the noun for taking your leave, and the house-word it is related to
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
You are talking to a colleague about a plan the two of you share — which we-word do you reach for? (\textbf{\ta{நாம்}}.) And which noun names the act of leaving rather than promising a return?
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[oru muṟai maṭṭum]{(the fifteen that came once) — the last page}

\label{lesson:TA-R86-the-last-page}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\ta{உ}}, then \textbf{\ta{ய}}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built, and what this page does with it}]
Everything here has come round twice in your reading: once where it was taught, once on a retrieval page in this last stretch. A second pass is where memory starts holding without the book, and the widest gap on offer runs from the opening pages to this one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Script: three pieces, one of them yours to draw}
\textbf{\ta{உ}} standing · \textbf{\ta{ி}} hanging · \textbf{\ta{ய}} a consonant · \textbf{\ta{ஒ}} standing o · \textbf{\ta{ோ}} the sign built from two marks.

Read these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ta{உ}}, and say whether it is a letter or a sign
  \item \textbf{\ta{ி}}, and say what it replaces
  \item \textbf{\ta{ஒ}} and \textbf{\ta{ோ}} — the same vowel standing, then hanging
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
\textbf{\ta{சரி}} · \textbf{\ta{பெயர்}} · \textbf{\ta{இருக்கிறீர்கள்}} · \textbf{\ta{போ}} · \textbf{\ta{ஒன்று}}

No glosses this time. Read each one and say what it means before moving on. The long one in the middle is the test: eight pieces, and you have met every piece.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{The exchange — five of them, unprompted}
The book opened with five, and an examiner opens with the same ones:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item greet, and answer a thank-you
  \item trade names, both sides, closing warmly
  \item ask after the person, and reply in full
  \item take your leave, promising the next meeting
  \item say what you speak, and what you do
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Page covered.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} exchange 2 above, both sides
  \item \emph{Say it:} exchange 3 above, both sides
  \item \emph{Say it:} exchange 1, then exchange 4, back to back
  \item \emph{Say it:} exchange 5, about yourself
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ta{சரி}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which sign on this page wraps around its consonant on both sides? (\textbf{\ta{ோ}}.) And which of the five exchanges would you want one more run at before somebody asks for it cold?
\end{tcolorbox}
